claim: The three accused jointly charged with one count of murder
requested_remedy: The three accused jointly charged with one count of murder
parties: Defendant: MOK TSAN-PING, SEE CHEUNG-SHUN, CHENG PO

facts.F1: The three accused are charged with murdering a man by stabbing him to death.
facts.F2: The prosecution’s case against them is that they, acting in pursuance of a joint enterprise, murdered the man.
facts.F3: The defence submission is that the Bill of Rights and/or the Basic Law have changed the common law so that the mental element for murder is no longer an intention either to kill or to cause grievous bodily harm i.e. really serious injury, but has become instead an intention either to kill or to endanger life.
facts.F4: The defence relies on two decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada, namely Vaillancourt v R (1988) 47 DLR (4th) 399 and R v Martineau (1990) 58 CCC 353.
facts.F5: The case of Vaillancourt deals with the constitutionality of a section of the Canadian Criminal Code that made it murder to cause death while committing or attempting to commit robbery, whether or not the person meant to cause death or knew that death was likely to be caused.
facts.F6: The case of Martineau deals with the constitutionality of a section of the Canadian Criminal Code that made it murder to cause death while committing or attempting to commit certain offences, including robbery, if the person meant to cause bodily harm for the purpose of facilitating the commission of the offence or facilitating flight after committing or attempting to commit the offence.
facts.F7: The Hong Kong provisions on which the defence places reliance are those in the Bill of Rights and the Basic Law which are equivalent to s. 7 and s. 11(d) of the Canadian Charter, including article 5 and article 10 of the Bill of Rights and article 28 and article 87 of the Basic Law.
facts.F8: Constructive murder, which did not involve intention to kill or cause really serious injury, has long since ceased to be part of the law of Hong Kong.
facts.F9: Vaillancourt and Martineau struck down constructive murder.
facts.F10: The mental element of murder as presently understood does not offend against the principles of the liberty and security of the person or the presumption of innocence.
facts.F11: The court held that mere foresight of death or serious bodily harm is not enough for a secondary party to a joint enterprise to be guilty of murder.

reference_issues: Whether the definition of the mental element of murder as an intention to kill or cause really serious injury is compatible with the Bill of Rights and/or the Basic Law.

The Basic Law
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

facts.F4: The Statement of Claim was served a few days after the Writ, but no medical reports supporting the claim were served.

facts.F6: The Plaintiff's claim against the First Defendant was dismissed by consent on 12th October 1995.

facts.F11: Expert medical opinion had to be gathered by the Second Defendant to assist him in defending the action.
